In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
TPA is an important factor in the initiation and promotion of carcinogenesis in mouse skin.

the carcinogen DMRA acts in two ways: (1) it causes a permanent damage to DNA in the epidermal basal cells, and (2) it induces a stationary hyperplastic reaction in the skin, which is characterized by a high rate of DNA synthesis in the epidermis.
a stationary hyperplastic state, with high rates of synthesis of DNA, RNA, proteins, lipids, carbohydrates, and other substances, must be considered as a very important co-factor in carcinogenesis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a stationary epidermal hyperplasia is a prerequisite for the initiation-promotion of tumour development.

the carcinogenic effect of the carcinogen DMRA in the initiation-promotion experiment is not only dependent on the dose, the duration and the time of application but is also dependent on a preceding induction of a stationary, non-inflammatory hyperplasia with a correspondingly high rate of DNA synthesis.
the tumour-promoting effect of TPA can be explained as an effect on the proliferation of the basal cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of a stationary hyperproliferation of the epidermis, induced by TPA, as an experimental model for the study of the initiation-promotion process of carcinogenesis in mouse skin has a high predictive value for the carcinogenicity of substances in the human organism.
the TPA-DMB-TPA scheme is a useful tool for studying epidermal carcinogenicity.
we have developed a method that allows us to measure and control the amount of TPA applied to the mouse skin.
